sources.title: Ibn al-Nafis's own Commentary on Anatomy in Avicenna's Canon (Sharh Tashrih al-Qanun), containing his description of pulmonary circulation

Later medical-historical scholarship (rediscovered in the 20th century) establishing Ibn al-Nafis's description of pulmonary circulation as predating William Harvey's better-known 17th-century European account by roughly 300 years

independent_thinking.rationale: Explicitly rejected Galen's long-authoritative theory that blood passes directly between the heart's ventricles through invisible pores, proposing instead that blood travels from the right ventricle to the left via the lungs (pulmonary circulation), documented directly via his own surviving commentary text and its explicit, reasoned departure from the Galenic model that had gone unchallenged for roughly a millennium.

analytical_rigor.rationale: Supported the pulmonary-circulation claim with specific anatomical reasoning about the structure of the heart's septum and the lungs, documented directly via the surviving argumentative structure of his own commentary text.

systems_abstraction.rationale: Reorganized and systematically re-examined Avicenna's entire anatomical framework in the Canon commentary rather than addressing isolated errors, inferred as strong systems-level revision from the documented comprehensive scope of the commentary project as a whole.

mastery_orientation.rationale: Produced an extensive multi-volume medical encyclopedia (Al-Shamil fi al-Tibb) in addition to his anatomical commentary, inferred as sustained deep engagement with the full breadth of contemporary medical knowledge from the documented scale of this separate major surviving work.

curiosity.rationale: Wrote on subjects beyond clinical medicine including logic and Islamic jurisprudence, inferred as some real intellectual range from the documented existence of these additional surviving works alongside his primary medical corpus.

provenance.notes: Roster-1000 session 12: West Asia diversity pick, physician occupation.
